newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU leaders see long haul on single currency dispute.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders see long haul on single currency dispute.

text.p: European Union leaders arrived Sunday ahead of a crucial two-day summit meant to help move the 15-nation bloc into the next century but which could be dominated by a dispute over plans for a single currency.
Germany and France, the driving forces behind EU moves toward the single currency, due to be launched in January 1999, have fallen into a dispute over how best to achieve it.

New French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has told his partners he is hostile to the economic austerity measures required to qualify for economic and monetary union and wants a new EU treaty to give a bigger profile to creating jobs.
He stunned EU officials last week by demanding more time to study the so-called stability pact, a framework for keeping EU budget deficits from ballooning after the currency, the euro, is introduced.

On the eve of the summit, Germany turned up the heat on its partners by ruling out costly Europe-wide job creation schemes, denting the normally strong Franco-German alliance at the heart of Europe and casting a pall over the meeting.
As ministers flew into the Dutch capital late on Sunday, all talk of reviewing plans to enlarge the EU was usurped by the trouble brewing over the single currency.
Germany vehemently opposes any weakening of the single currency criteria and any job creation schemes that involve pumping huge sums of public cash into big finance projects.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, architect of the stability pact and a staunch advocate of budget discipline, said on arriving that he would not accept any new spending to meet French demands for a new focus on boosting growth and jobs.
He insisted, too, that a pact limiting budget deficits of countries joining the euro was not negotiable.

"The stability pact is not up for negotiation," he said. "We will stick to our position that there will be no money flowing from Germany for additional jobs creation programmes," he told Reuters earlier.
Other leaders tried to be upbeat.
European Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy said he believed there would be an agreement on the stability pact either on Sunday or Monday.

"There is a will to succeed. Either tonight or tomorrow there will be a solution," he told a news conference shortly before EU finance ministers were due to hold an informal dinner to discuss the issue.
Luxembourg Premier Jean-Claude Juncker, who brokered an initial deal between France and Germany on budget discipline last December, said he believed there would be success at the summit.
Asked whether he had been negotiating with Paris and Bonn over the new dispute, he replied: "I had sufficient contact in order to know that we will have success."
Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink said he expected the summit to reach agreement on the stability pact but did not rule out negotiations continuing until Tuesday.
An EU diplomat said the problem for the leaders was to find a way of dealing with French demands to resurrect funding for communications projects to create jobs.
Another diplomat said leaders could offer France some hope by promising pilot projects involving getting younger people into jobs and paid for out of existing funds.
